statement: A translation vector $\mathbf{v}$ is a fixed vector that specifies the displacement of every point of an object or space under a translation function $T_{\mathbf{v}}$, defined by $T_{\mathbf{v}}(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}$ (or coordinate-wise in three dimensions by $(x, y, z) \to (x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y, z + \Delta z)$ where $(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)$ is the translation vector common to all points).

symbols.meaning: fixed translation vector specifying the direction, sense, and length of displacement
initial position vector of an object or point
translation transformation/function associated with translation vector \mathbf{v}
subset or geometric figure undergoing translation

properties.property: The composition of translations corresponds to the addition of their translation vectors: $T_{\mathbf{v}} T_{\mathbf{w}} = T_{\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}}$
properties.why: consecutive displacements by constant vectors add vectorially

properties.property: The inverse translation is obtained by negating the translation vector: $T_{\mathbf{v}}^{-1} = T_{-\mathbf{v}}$
properties.why: reversing the direction of the vector inverts the displacement

properties.property: Translations commute ($T_{\mathbf{v}} T_{\mathbf{w}} = T_{\mathbf{w}} T_{\mathbf{v}}$), and the set of all translations forms an abelian group
A translation is an isometry that preserves lengths of line segments, directions, and amplitudes of angles
properties.why: every point is displaced by the exact same distance and direction without rotation

properties.property: The translate of a subset $A$ by $T_{\mathbf{v}}$ is given by $A + \mathbf{v}$
properties.why: the translation function applies the constant vector addition to each element of the subset

properties.property: A translation in $n$ dimensions can be represented linearly as matrix multiplication in $(n+1)$-dimensional homogeneous coordinates
properties.why: translations have no fixed points, whereas standard linear matrix multiplication always fixes the origin

assumptions.assumption: The displacement vector is uniform and identical for every point of the object or figure
assumptions.breaks_when: different points undergo differing displacements, as occurs in rotational motion or non-rigid body deformations

assumptions.assumption: The transformation occurs in a Euclidean space or affine vector space where vector addition is defined
assumptions.breaks_when: the underlying space is curved or non-Euclidean without a well-defined global constant vector addition

failure_modes.mode: Attempting to represent a non-zero translation using a standard $n \times n$ matrix in Cartesian coordinates
failure_modes.signature: The origin remains fixed ($M \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$), failing to translate points away from the origin
failure_modes.cause: Linear transformations on $\mathbb{R}^n$ must fix the origin, whereas translations with $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$ have no fixed points; augmented homogeneous coordinates are required

failure_modes.mode: Conflating active geometric translation of an object with passive translation of axes
failure_modes.signature: Coordinates of the transformed object have the inverted sign ($-\mathbf{v}$ instead of $+\mathbf{v}$)
failure_modes.cause: A passive translation shifts the coordinate frame while keeping the object stationary, which is inverse to displacing the object within a fixed coordinate frame
